hero.description: Walk the peninsula slowly enough to read Luang Prabang as a living town: monasteries, timber houses, colonial-era buildings and two rivers compressed into a compact World Heritage landscape.
steps: Start before the main street gets busy
Use side lanes as much as the main axis
Pause at temples without treating them as a checklist
Finish beside either the Mekong or Nam Khan
hero.rhythmNote: The transitions between houses, temples, riverbanks and everyday street life are the point, not the number of monuments collected.
hero.photoNote: Historic peninsula · Mekong and Nam Khan

route.secondary: peninsula between the Mekong and Nam Khan

budget.secondary: selected temples and museums may charge

chapters.label: THE TOWN
chapters.title: The heritage is in the mixture, not one building
chapters.body: UNESCO protects Luang Prabang for the unusually coherent meeting of traditional Lao urban fabric with architecture introduced during the colonial period. On foot, that relationship is easy to read: monastery compounds sit beside timber houses, masonry shophouses and quieter residential lanes, while the rivers keep the peninsula legible.

chapters.label: THE PACE
chapters.title: Walk early, then let the route loosen
chapters.body: Use the main heritage street as a spine, then step into side lanes and river edges. Respect monastery space, avoid blocking residents, and remember that the old town is still lived in rather than preserved as an open-air museum.

note.label: ATLAS NOTE
note.text: If you only have one free morning in Luang Prabang, this is the activity that gives the rest of the city context.

items.label: Start
items.detail: Use the two rivers as natural boundaries and the central heritage street as orientation.

items.label: Time needed
items.detail: Long enough to enter a few temple compounds without turning the morning into a monument checklist.

items.label: Best time
items.detail: Cooler temperatures and softer street activity make walking more comfortable.

items.label: Temple etiquette
items.detail: Cover shoulders and knees in sacred spaces and keep voices low.

faq.question: Do I need a guide for the Luang Prabang heritage walk?
faq.answer: No. The historic peninsula is compact and easy to explore independently, though a knowledgeable local guide can add architectural and religious context.

faq.question: How long should I allow?
faq.answer: Two to three hours is a good first walk, with more time if you add major temples or the Royal Palace Museum.

faq.question: What should I wear?
faq.answer: Light walking clothes are fine, but cover shoulders and knees when entering temple compounds or prayer halls.

faq.question: Is early morning best?
faq.answer: Early morning is excellent for cooler streets and a quieter atmosphere; late afternoon is also comfortable.

faq.question: What should I look for?
faq.answer: Look at the relationship between monasteries, traditional Lao houses, colonial-era buildings and the two riverfronts rather than only named monuments.

seo.title: Luang Prabang Heritage Walk | Things To Do Atlas
seo.description: Walk Luang Prabang’s UNESCO peninsula with a practical 2–3 hour route, temple etiquette and a slower way to read the old town.

hero.description: Study one of Luang Prabang’s clearest architectural statements: low-sweeping roofs, mosaic work and royal ceremonial buildings in a compact monastery compound.
steps: Enter without rushing the main sim
Walk the exterior before going inside
Find the Tree of Life mosaic
hero.rhythmNote: The complex is compact but visually dense. One slow hour is more useful than ten fast photographs.
hero.photoNote: Northern tip of the historic peninsula

time.secondary: longer if you study the mosaics

route.secondary: near the meeting of the two rivers

chapters.label: THE SIM
chapters.title: Start with the roof before the ornament
chapters.body: The main ordination hall is defined by a layered roof that sweeps unusually low toward the ground. Step back far enough to read the silhouette before focusing on gilded details; the building’s proportions explain why Wat Xieng Thong is such an important reference point for Luang Prabang architecture.

chapters.label: THE DETAILS
chapters.title: The complex rewards a second circuit
chapters.body: After the main hall, look for the coloured-glass Tree of Life mosaic and the funerary-carriage building. Architecture, ritual and royal history overlap here, so the secondary structures are not side notes.

note.label: ATLAS NOTE
note.text: Go early if you want the architecture to feel calm rather than crowded.

items.label: Time needed
items.detail: Enough for the main sim, mosaics and funerary-carriage building without rushing.

items.label: Getting there
items.detail: It fits naturally at the far end of an old-town walk.

items.label: Entry
items.detail: Entrance fees can change; confirm the current ticket at the site.

items.label: Dress
items.detail: Cover shoulders and knees, remove shoes where indicated and keep voices low.

faq.question: Why is Wat Xieng Thong important?
faq.answer: It is one of Luang Prabang’s best-known monasteries and a major example of the city’s temple architecture, with strong royal associations.

faq.question: How long do I need?
faq.answer: Around one hour is a good minimum.

faq.question: What should I make sure to see?
faq.answer: The main sim, Tree of Life mosaic and funerary-carriage building are the three deliberate stops.

faq.question: When should I go?
faq.answer: Morning is usually the easiest time for cooler temperatures and a calmer atmosphere.

faq.question: Can I combine it with other sights?
faq.answer: Yes. It sits naturally at the end of a peninsula walk and pairs well with the Mekong and Nam Khan riverfronts.

seo.title: Wat Xieng Thong Luang Prabang | Things To Do Atlas
seo.description: Plan a focused visit to Wat Xieng Thong: rooflines, mosaics, time needed, temple etiquette and how it fits into Luang Prabang.

hero.description: Climb the central sacred hill to make Luang Prabang legible from above, with temple stops on the way and views across the Mekong, Nam Khan and old-town roofs.
steps: Choose one side for the climb
Use the summit view to read both rivers
hero.rhythmNote: Sunset is famous but crowded. If the view matters more than the social scene, go earlier or choose morning light.

route.secondary: central access from the old town

chapters.label: THE CLIMB
chapters.title: Treat the hill as a route
chapters.body: Phou Si rises directly from the historic centre, so the climb passes religious structures and smaller viewpoints before the top. Take the stairs steadily and give those intermediate spaces attention instead of seeing them only as obstacles.

chapters.label: THE VIEW
chapters.title: The summit explains the shape of Luang Prabang
chapters.body: From above, the narrow town, surrounding hills and two rivers become much easier to understand. Sunset gives the classic atmosphere but also the heaviest concentration of visitors.

note.label: ATLAS NOTE
note.text: Choose Phou Si for orientation, not solitude.

items.label: Time needed
items.detail: Allow time for the stairs, temple pauses and summit.

items.label: Best time
items.detail: Sunset is atmospheric but busy.

items.label: Access
items.detail: There are multiple approaches through town.

items.label: Bring
items.detail: Heat and wet steps can make the climb more tiring than the distance suggests.

faq.question: Is Phou Si difficult to climb?
faq.answer: It is a stair climb rather than a technical hike. Most visitors can manage it with steady pauses.

faq.question: Is sunset worth it?
faq.answer: Yes for atmosphere, but it is also the busiest period. Morning gives more space.

faq.question: How long should I allow?
faq.answer: Plan one to two hours including the climb and summit.

faq.question: Do I need hiking gear?
faq.answer: No. Normal walking shoes with decent grip and water are enough for most conditions.

faq.question: What can I see from the top?
faq.answer: The old-town roofs, Mekong, Nam Khan and surrounding hills are the main orientation points.

seo.title: Phou Si Mountain Luang Prabang | Things To Do Atlas
seo.description: Plan the Phou Si climb in Luang Prabang: timing, crowds, stair effort and what the summit view reveals.

hero.description: Use the former Royal Palace to connect Luang Prabang’s ceremonial role, monarchy and national history with the urban landscape outside.
steps: Use the palace rooms for context
hero.rhythmNote: This is a context stop rather than a photo-heavy one; museum rules can shape the pace.

chapters.label: THE PALACE
chapters.title: Place Luang Prabang in modern Lao history
chapters.body: The palace was built for the Luang Prabang royal family in the early twentieth century and today functions as a museum. Its collections and ceremonial spaces help explain why Luang Prabang remained symbolically important after political power shifted elsewhere.

chapters.label: THE VISIT
chapters.title: Expect museum rules to shape the pace
chapters.body: Opening schedules, bag rules, photography restrictions and room access can change, so check locally before committing a tight itinerary.

note.label: ATLAS NOTE
note.text: Visit early in your stay if you care about history; the rest of Luang Prabang will make more sense afterward.

items.label: Time needed
items.detail: Enough to move through the museum without rushing.

items.label: Opening
items.detail: Schedules and closure periods can change.

items.label: Entry
items.detail: Confirm current admission at the museum.

items.label: Museum rules
items.detail: Photography, bags or room access may be controlled.

faq.question: Is the Royal Palace Museum worth visiting?
faq.answer: Yes if you want historical context for Luang Prabang and the former monarchy.

faq.question: How long do I need?
faq.answer: Allow one to two hours.

faq.question: Can I take photos inside?
faq.answer: Do not assume so. Follow the current signs and staff instructions.

faq.question: When should I visit?
faq.answer: Morning is a sensible choice because schedules can include closure periods later in the day.

faq.question: What should I combine it with?
faq.answer: Phou Si, the heritage walk and nearby temples fit naturally around it.

seo.title: Royal Palace Museum Luang Prabang | Things To Do Atlas
seo.description: Plan Luang Prabang’s Royal Palace Museum: why it matters, how long to allow and the museum-rule cautions worth knowing.

hero.description: Observe the dawn alms procession as a living Buddhist practice, keeping enough distance that your visit does not turn a daily religious ritual into a performance.
steps: Do not use flash or block the line
Participate only if you understand the etiquette
hero.rhythmNote: Watching respectfully is better than participating badly. If unsure, simply observe from a distance.

chapters.label: THE PRACTICE
chapters.title: This is daily religious practice
chapters.body: Monastics receive food offerings from laypeople as part of an ongoing religious relationship. The most useful visitor rule is simple: do nothing that changes the ceremony for the people taking part.

chapters.label: YOUR ROLE
chapters.title: Observation is a complete way to attend
chapters.body: Stand back, keep noise low, avoid flash and never obstruct the line of monks or local donors. If you choose to give alms, learn the local practice first.

note.label: ATLAS NOTE
note.text: A quiet observer is not missing the experience. Respect is the experience.

items.label: Timing
items.detail: Exact timing shifts with season; ask locally the evening before.

items.label: Best approach
items.detail: Participation is optional.

items.label: Photography
items.detail: Do not step into the route or crowd monks and donors.

items.label: If participating
items.detail: Use appropriate offerings and follow local guidance.

faq.question: Can tourists watch Tak Bat?
faq.answer: Yes, but watch quietly from a respectful distance and avoid actions that alter the procession.

faq.question: Do I need to give alms?
faq.answer: No. Observation is completely valid.

faq.question: Can I take photos?
faq.answer: Yes only with restraint: no flash, no blocking and no close intrusion.

faq.question: What time does it happen?
faq.answer: Very early in the morning around dawn; confirm locally because timing varies through the year.

faq.question: What should I wear?
faq.answer: Dress conservatively, covering shoulders and knees.

seo.title: Tak Bat Morning Alms Luang Prabang | Things To Do Atlas
seo.description: Understand Luang Prabang’s morning alms procession before you go: respectful observation, photography etiquette and timing.

hero.description: Leave town for Kuang Si’s limestone cascades and turquoise forest pools, one of the famous Luang Prabang day trips that still rewards taking your time beyond the main viewpoint.
hero.rhythmNote: The site becomes busier as the day builds. Early arrival improves both the forest walk and the pools.

chapters.label: THE WATER
chapters.title: The lower pools are part of the attraction
chapters.body: Kuang Si is a tiered waterfall system rather than one single drop. Pale-blue pools and smaller cascades create the first half of the visit before the larger main waterfall comes into view.

chapters.label: THE DAY
chapters.title: Early arrival makes a famous place feel better
chapters.body: Leaving early reduces crowd pressure at the pools, gives cooler walking conditions and leaves flexibility to stop rather than moving with the busiest midday wave.

note.label: ATLAS NOTE
note.text: Do not judge Kuang Si only by the main waterfall. The forest and sequence of pools are what make the half day work.

items.label: Time needed
items.detail: Allow road time plus two to three hours around the falls.

items.label: Best time
items.detail: Earlier arrival means cooler walking and fewer people.

items.label: Entry
items.detail: Confirm current entrance and transport prices locally.

items.label: Swimming
items.detail: Follow current signs and staff guidance because conditions vary.

faq.question: How much time do I need at Kuang Si?
faq.answer: Plan a half day from Luang Prabang.

faq.question: Can I swim at Kuang Si?
faq.answer: Swimming is possible in designated pools when conditions allow; follow current signs.

faq.question: What is the best time to go?
faq.answer: Morning is the strongest all-round choice for cooler weather and fewer crowds.

faq.question: How do I get there?
faq.answer: Shared minivans, tuk-tuks, private cars and organised transfers are common options from Luang Prabang.

faq.question: Does it always look bright blue?
faq.answer: No. Water colour and clarity vary with rainfall, flow and season.

seo.title: Kuang Si Waterfalls from Luang Prabang | Things To Do Atlas
seo.description: Plan a Kuang Si half day from Luang Prabang: timing, swimming rules, transport and seasonal water conditions.

hero.description: Travel north to the limestone caves above the Mekong–Nam Ou confluence, where generations of Buddha images make the visit a religious and cultural site rather than a conventional cave excursion.
steps: Continue to the upper cave if open
hero.rhythmNote: The boat journey is part of the classic experience; by road the caves remain worthwhile but the half day feels different.

route.secondary: river approach is slower and scenic

chapters.label: THE CAVES
chapters.title: Two caves, two atmospheres
chapters.body: The lower cave opens toward the river and receives natural light, while the upper cave is darker and requires more effort to reach. The Buddha images are devotional objects accumulated over generations.

chapters.label: THE JOURNEY
chapters.title: Boat and road create different half days
chapters.body: The traditional approach is upstream on the Mekong, making the river journey part of the visit. Road transport is faster if time is limited.

note.label: ATLAS NOTE
note.text: If you choose the boat, judge the outing as a river day with caves in the middle.

items.label: Time needed
items.detail: Boat travel makes the outing longer than road access.

items.label: Access
items.detail: The river approach gives the classic arrival below the cliff.

items.label: Light
items.detail: The upper cave is dark and steps can be uneven.

items.label: Entry
items.detail: Transport and cave admission are separate.

faq.question: Should I go by boat or road?
faq.answer: Choose boat if the Mekong journey is part of what you want; road is faster if you mainly want the caves.

faq.question: How long does the visit take?
faq.answer: Allow a half day from Luang Prabang.

faq.question: What is inside the caves?
faq.answer: They are known for large numbers of Buddha images placed there over generations.

faq.question: Do I need a flashlight?
faq.answer: A small torch is useful for the darker upper cave.

faq.question: Is it mainly a natural attraction?
faq.answer: No. Its religious significance and Buddha-image tradition are central to the experience.

seo.title: Pak Ou Caves from Luang Prabang | Things To Do Atlas
seo.description: Plan Pak Ou Caves by boat or road: cave layout, Buddha-image tradition, lighting, time needed and practical access.

hero.description: Use Wat Visoun as a counterpoint to Luang Prabang’s more ornate temples, with the distinctive rounded That Makmo stupa giving the compound its visual identity.
steps: Read the main hall at distance
hero.rhythmNote: This is a strong one-hour context stop, especially after Wat Xieng Thong.

chapters.label: THE TEMPLE
chapters.title: Use Wat Visoun as a contrast
chapters.body: The compound feels broader and plainer than highly decorative Xieng Thong. That contrast helps you see how different periods and forms coexist within Luang Prabang’s religious landscape.

chapters.label: THE STUPA
chapters.title: That Makmo is the strongest marker
chapters.body: The rounded stupa beside the temple gives the site an unmistakable silhouette. Walk around it slowly rather than relying on one frontal view.

note.label: ATLAS NOTE
note.text: Pair it with Xieng Thong if you want one clear architectural contrast.

items.label: Time needed
items.detail: Enough for the main hall, stupa and compound.

items.label: Getting there
items.detail: Easy to combine with other central cultural stops.

items.label: Entry
items.detail: Confirm current admission locally.

items.label: Etiquette
items.detail: Dress appropriately and avoid disrupting prayer or monastic activity.

faq.question: Why visit Wat Visoun after Xieng Thong?
faq.answer: Because the two sites feel different and provide a useful architectural contrast.

faq.question: What is That Makmo?
faq.answer: It is the distinctive rounded stupa associated with the Wat Visoun compound.

faq.question: How long do I need?
faq.answer: Around 45 to 60 minutes.

faq.question: Is it walkable from the old town?
faq.answer: Yes for most visitors, or it is a very short ride.

faq.question: When is the best time?
faq.answer: Morning is comfortable and easy to combine with other cultural stops.

seo.title: Wat Visoun Luang Prabang | Things To Do Atlas
seo.description: Visit Wat Visoun and That Makmo in Luang Prabang: why the temple matters, how long to stay and how it contrasts with Xieng Thong.

hero.description: Spend an hour with the history and continuing impact of unexploded ordnance in Laos, then leave with a clearer understanding of why clearance work still matters far beyond the museum walls.
steps: Focus on civilian impact and present-day work
hero.rhythmNote: This is not military memorabilia. The useful focus is civilian impact, clearance and risk education.

chapters.label: THE CONTEXT
chapters.title: A past war with a present footprint
chapters.body: The centre explains how unexploded ordnance continues to affect communities, agriculture and development in Laos decades after the conflict period.

chapters.label: THE WORK
chapters.title: Clearance is still current
chapters.body: The strongest part of the visit is understanding what survey, clearance and risk-education teams actually do and why this remains a public-safety issue.

note.label: ATLAS NOTE
note.text: One hour here changes how you understand rural Laos more than another generic museum stop would.

items.label: Time needed
items.detail: Enough for the displays and video material without rushing.

items.label: Cost
items.detail: Check on site for donation or support options.

items.label: Getting there
items.detail: Combine it with another southern-town stop.

items.label: Rural safety
items.detail: Stay on established paths and follow local warnings.

faq.question: What is the UXO Lao Visitor Centre about?
faq.answer: It explains the history and continuing impact of unexploded ordnance, including clearance work and risk education.

faq.question: How long should I spend there?
faq.answer: Around one hour is enough for most visitors.

faq.question: Is it suitable for children?
faq.answer: The subject includes war and civilian harm, so adults should judge based on age and sensitivity.

faq.question: Does UXO still matter in Laos today?
faq.answer: Yes. Survey, clearance and risk-education programmes remain active.

faq.question: What should travellers remember in rural areas?
faq.answer: Stay on established routes and never touch unfamiliar metal objects or suspected ordnance.

seo.title: UXO Lao Visitor Centre Luang Prabang | Things To Do Atlas
seo.description: Visit the UXO Lao Visitor Centre for clear context on unexploded ordnance, current clearance work and practical rural safety.

hero.description: Use this compact museum to move beyond generic labels and understand textiles, objects and cultural practices through more specific ethnic and community contexts.
steps: Follow objects back to named communities
Use the shop as an extension, not the main event
hero.rhythmNote: The museum is small enough to rush and good enough not to. Read the labels; the context is the value.

chapters.label: THE LABELS
chapters.title: Specificity is the point
chapters.body: The museum’s strength is that objects are connected to named communities, techniques and social uses rather than collapsed into a vague image of ethnic Laos.

chapters.label: THE TEXTILES
chapters.title: Technique and identity sit together
chapters.body: Pattern, fibre, dye, production method and when a garment is worn can all carry meaning. TAEC is useful before craft visits because it gives you better questions to ask later.

note.label: ATLAS NOTE
note.text: If you are going to buy textiles in Laos, spend an hour here first.

items.label: Time needed
items.detail: The galleries are compact, but interpretation carries much of the value.

items.label: Approach
items.detail: This is about cultural context, not only visually striking textiles.

items.label: Tours & workshops
items.detail: Some activities may require advance booking.

items.label: Pair it with
items.detail: TAEC works well before Ock Pop Tok or Ban Xang Khong.

faq.question: How long do I need at TAEC?
faq.answer: About one hour is a good planning estimate.

faq.question: What will I see?
faq.answer: Textiles, clothing, jewellery, tools, domestic objects and interpretation introducing the diversity of ethnic cultures in Laos.

faq.question: Is it mainly a textile museum?
faq.answer: Textiles are important, but the museum is broader and focuses on cultural context and material life.

faq.question: Is it worth going before a weaving village?
faq.answer: Yes. It gives useful context and vocabulary that make later craft visits more meaningful.

faq.question: Can I walk there from central Luang Prabang?
faq.answer: Yes. It is a central-town museum and easy to combine with an old-town day.

seo.title: Traditional Arts and Ethnology Centre Luang Prabang | Things To Do Atlas
seo.description: Visit TAEC in Luang Prabang for careful context on Laos’s ethnic communities, textiles and material culture.

aliases: Ock Pop Tok Living Crafts Centre
hero.description: See weaving and natural-dye work in a living craft setting beside the Mekong, where understanding process and makers matters more than treating textiles as anonymous souvenirs.
steps: Ask how dyes and fibres are prepared
Book a class only if you want hands-on depth
hero.rhythmNote: You do not need to buy anything for the visit to work. Use the centre to understand labour, technique and provenance.
hero.photoNote: Mekong-side craft centre south of town

chapters.label: THE PROCESS
chapters.title: The loom is only one part of the textile
chapters.body: A good visit follows the material backwards: fibre preparation, natural dyes, pattern planning and weaving all shape the finished cloth. Asking about preparation reveals how much labour sits behind one piece.

chapters.label: THE PURCHASE
chapters.title: Provenance is more useful than bargaining
chapters.body: If you buy, ask who made the textile, what fibre and dye were used and whether the piece was produced locally. Traceable production gives you a better basis for judging value than appearance alone.

note.label: ATLAS NOTE
note.text: This is the stronger choice when you want to understand how Lao textiles are made, not simply where to buy them.

items.label: Visit format
items.detail: Check current workshop schedules if hands-on weaving or dyeing is the priority.

items.label: Time needed
items.detail: Allow longer for a workshop.

items.label: Buying
items.detail: Use maker and production information to understand what you are paying for.

items.label: Transport
items.value: Short ride from the heritage centre
items.detail: A bike, tuk-tuk or other short ride is usually more practical than walking in heat.

faq.question: Do I have to book a workshop?
faq.answer: No. The Living Crafts Centre can be visited without taking a class.

faq.question: How long should I allow?
faq.answer: One to two hours works for a normal visit; workshops require longer.

faq.question: Is it mainly a shop?
faq.answer: No. The strongest reason to visit is understanding textile production; shopping is optional.

faq.question: What can I learn there?
faq.answer: Weaving, natural dyes, fibre preparation and the labour behind finished Lao textiles.

faq.question: Is it walkable from the old town?
faq.answer: It is south of the main heritage core, so a short ride is usually more practical.

seo.title: Ock Pop Tok Living Crafts Centre Luang Prabang | Things To Do Atlas
seo.description: Visit Ock Pop Tok in Luang Prabang for weaving, natural dyes and practical context on workshops and textile provenance.

hero.description: Take a short ride from town for a craft-focused village stop associated with silk weaving and saa-paper work, looking for working processes rather than only finished products.
steps: Look for active looms and paper work
Buy only when you understand what is locally made
hero.rhythmNote: This is a lived-in village, not an open-air museum. Keep the visit small and ask before entering workspaces.
hero.photoNote: Short ride from central Luang Prabang

chapters.label: THE CRAFT
chapters.title: Look for process, not just shelves
chapters.body: The useful reason to visit is seeing how textiles or saa paper move from raw material toward a finished object. Active looms, fibre preparation and paper drying tell you more than a wall of completed scarves.

chapters.label: THE VILLAGE
chapters.title: Do not turn homes into exhibits
chapters.body: This is an ordinary settlement with families, traffic and private spaces. Stay on public routes unless invited in and ask before photographing people or work areas.

note.label: ATLAS NOTE
note.text: Come here for the scale of a working craft village; use TAEC or Ock Pop Tok for deeper interpretation.

items.label: Time needed
items.detail: Enough for a short craft-focused visit.

items.label: Timing
items.detail: Go when workshops and family businesses are likely to be active.

items.label: Photography
items.detail: A workshop may also be someone’s home or workplace.

items.label: Buying
items.detail: Ask who made an item and where rather than assuming every product was produced on site.

faq.question: How long do I need in Ban Xang Khong?
faq.answer: One to two hours is enough for a short craft-focused visit.

faq.question: What crafts is the village associated with?
faq.answer: It is commonly associated with handwoven textiles and saa-paper making.

faq.question: Do I have to buy something?
faq.answer: No. Buying is optional.

faq.question: Can I photograph workshops?
faq.answer: Ask first, especially when people, homes or private work areas are in the frame.

faq.question: Is it the same as Ock Pop Tok?
faq.answer: No. Ban Xang Khong is an informal working-village stop; Ock Pop Tok provides a more structured craft centre.

seo.title: Ban Xang Khong Weaving Village Luang Prabang | Things To Do Atlas
seo.description: Plan a respectful Ban Xang Khong visit for weaving and saa-paper craft, with practical notes on timing, photography and buying locally made work.
